title: Purification brings advantages in sequential quantum channel discrimination
authors: Zoe G. del Toro, Marco Túlio Quintino, Jessica Bavaresco
abstract: Purifications are often used as a convenient mathematical representation of quantum states and channels when constructing protocols for quantum information processing tasks. Although powerful, this perspective can suggest that the purifying degrees of freedom and its correlations with an environment are just a useful change of representation. Here we show how they can instead be exploited as an operational resource in sequential quantum channel discrimination, even when the environmental reference frame is unknown or averaged. In contrast to state discrimination and parallel channel discrimination, for which bare and averaged-purification access are equivalent, sequential access to purified resources exhibits a strict advantage in probability of success. We prove this strict separation via two main results. In the first, we construct a pair of families of qubit-qubit channels with a strict separation in the two-query case, and in the second, we show an example of a pair of qubit-qubit channels whose purifications are perfectly distinguishable with three queries while no finite number of bare (non-purified) queries suffices for perfect discrimination. These separations imply an advantage of sequential over parallel strategies for channel discrimination and establish the impossibility of converting bare channel queries into averaged-purification queries via transformations that allow arbitrary interventions between queries, strengthening previous results.
summary: This theoretical paper proves that in sequential quantum channel discrimination, utilizing the purification of a quantum channel provides a strict operational advantage over using the bare channel resource. The authors rigorously demonstrate this advantage using explicit constructions and by analyzing the limitations of converting bare queries into purified ones.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether accessing the purification of a quantum channel provides an operational advantage over accessing the bare channel resource, particularly in sequential quantum channel discrimination.
main_result: For sequential discrimination tasks, access to the purified resource yields a strict advantage in the probability of success compared to bare queries, and this advantage is not present for parallel strategies.
method: The authors analyze three distinct resource access models (bare, averaged purification, unknown purification) and use quantum information theory tools, including constructing specific sequential quantum testers and deriving upper/lower bounds on the success probability.
model_or_system: The model involves quantum channels $C: \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_I) 	o \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_O)$ and the concept of purification, which extends the system to an environment $\mathcal{H}_E$. The discrimination task compares the performance of these different resource accesses.
key_observables: The probability of success in quantum channel discrimination, quantified by the maximum average score achievable under different resource access models.
important_parameters: The number of queries ($k$), and the specific structure of the channels $C_0$ and $C_1$ used in the explicit constructions.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the mathematical framework of Stinespring dilation and the definition of linear, completely positive, and causal transformations between resource access models.
figures_summary: Figure 1 depicts the three channel access models ($R_1, R_2, R_3$), illustrating the different ways quantum resources can be accessed for channel discrimination.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical framework by defining the three resource access models and proving the hierarchy of convertibility. It then analyzes the performance in general quantum-to-classical tasks, showing equivalence for parallel strategies but strict advantage for sequential ones. Finally, it provides explicit constructions demonstrating this advantage for $k=2$ and $k=3$ queries.
why_interesting: The findings establish a clear operational hierarchy among quantum resources, suggesting that the mathematical concept of purification can be leveraged as a genuine, non-trivial resource in quantum information protocols.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Channel access models. Depiction of the three channel access models. Resource 1 corresponds to k inde- pendent queries of channel C, defined as R(k) bare(C) in Eq. (4). Resource 2 corresponds to the average over the environment of k queries of the same purification of channel C, defined as R(k) avg(C) in Eq. (5). Resource 3 corresponds to k queries of a fixed unknown purification of channel C, defined as R(k) ukn(C, U) in Eq. (6).

Figure 2. Implementation of two-query quantum testers with quantum circuits. Top: a quantum strategy for a quantum-to-classical task that acts on two queries of a channel resource either in parallel or sequentially, implemented by a quantum circuit. Bottom: the corresponding representation of these circuits as parallel and sequential quantum testers T(2) ∈PAR and T(2) ∈SEQ.

Figure 3. Discrimination advantage from purifications implies sequential advantage over parallel strategies (Corollary 2). Strict advantage in the two-query probability of successful discrimination for the channels in Theorem 1 under different access models: Bare queries access (R1) un- der parallel strategies (blue), bare queries access (R1) under sequential strategies (orange), and access to averaged purifica- tion (R2) under sequential strategies (green).

Figure 4. Implementation constraints of the transform- ation converting R1 into R2 (Corollary 3). The trans- formation ΛR17→R2 that can universally transform bare queries of a quantum channel R(k) bare(C) into the average of its puri- fications R(k) avg(C) can be implemented by a quantum parallel circuit (left) but not as a sequential quantum circuit that al- lows for arbitrary interventions in between queries. The image illustrates the case where k = m = 2.

Figure 5. Quantum-to-classical and quantum-to- quantum tasks. Top: Example of a quantum-to-classical task related to discrimination. In all quantum-to-classical tasks, access to fixed unknown purifications (left) and aver- aged purification (right) achieves equal performance. Bottom: Example of a quantum-to-quantum task where access to fixed unknown purifications (left) outperforms access to averaged purification (right). This task shows how the non-convertibility of these resources can be phrased in operational terms.
